Composite: Alamy/Getty/PA Competition and Markets Authority Trainline, Virgin Atlantic and Red Driving School investigated over hidden fees UK competition watchdog investigation is part of broader clampdown on illegal ‘drip pricing’ Business live – latest updates Lauren Almeida Wed 19 Aug 2026 07.14 EDT First published on Wed 19 Aug 2026 04.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The UK’s competition watchdog has launched investigations into Trainline, Virgin Atlantic and Red Driving School over concerns that all three companies displayed misleadingly low prices to their customers. The Competition and Markets Authority’s investigations are part of a broader clampdown on “drip pricing” , an illegal practice that makes a product appear cheaper by not including all mandatory fees. The regulator said it had opened investigations into the companies amid concerns that customers had not been shown the total price up front when buying train and coach tickets, holidays or driving lessons. “The first price customers see should be the price they pay,” said Emma Cochrane, the executive director for consumer protection at the CMA. “Clear pricing helps people compare offers confidently and choose the option that works best for them. “Unexpected mandatory charges make this much harder, which is why the CMA initially put these firms on notice over concerns about their pricing practices and is now opening formal investigations.” Trainline said in a statement to the stock exchange that it had “proactively engaged with the CMA over several months” and was “taking steps to enhance the presentation of certain fees”. Shares in the business, which is the only one of the three companies that is listed on the stock exchange, fell by as much as 14% in early trading on Wednesday. Virgin Atlantic said mandatory fees were “indicated at multiple stages” when customers were booking trips but it was reviewing the concerns and would cooperate with the regulator. Red Driving School said it valued transparency in its customer interactions and was engaging with the CMA. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion UK retailers too slow to pass on fuel price falls, watchdog says Read more The CMA’s investigations have been launched using its new consumer protection powers, which were granted last year. These powers allow the regulator to decide whether consumer laws have been broken, rather than having to go through the courts. If the CMA finds there has been an infringement of the law, it can order businesses to pay compensation to affected customers and can fine companies up to 10% of their global turnover. Earlier this year the CMA ordered the ticket seller StubHub to pay out nearly £1.5m in customer refunds and penalties for drip pricing. It also fined the AA £4.2m and ordered it to repay more than £760,000 to learner drivers over drip pricing. Andy Burnham has also promised to end “ rip-off ” business practices. Writing in the Guardian this month, the prime minister said his government would step in wherever it could , as he seeks to put the cost of living at the heart of his premiership. https://www.express.co.uk/news/uk/224975.text: Home News UK The Navy is at its smallest in living memory (Image: Getty) The First Sea Lord has warned Britannia must once again rule the waves to counter Russia — and that is why we should be concerned. In a startling admission, General Sir Gwyn Jenkins said Britain must “rediscover what it means to be a maritime nation” . This should serve as a piercing wake-up call for the Treasury as the drumbeat of Kremlin aggression grows louder. Our proud Royal Navy once set the standard — now we’re relying on allies to help us in our own backyard while Vladimir Putin becomes increasingly brazen. The protracted deployment of HMS Dragon to Cyprus earlier this year horribly exposed the Navy’s fragility, and it was only made to look worse by France amassing an armada in half the time. HMS Dragon's protracted deployment to Cyprus earlier this year sparked concerns (Image: Getty) After decades of cuts, the chickens are coming home to roost. Make no mistake, the state of the Navy is appalling and it’s little wonder Russia senses weakness. The Senior Service is at its smallest in living memory, with a measly five Type 23s making up the creaking frigate fleet. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Russian President Vladimir Putin (Image: Getty) The remaining ships, originally designed for the Cold War, entered service in the late 90s/early 2000s with an original 18-year lifespan. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT However, these ageing vessels are expected to remain in service until 2033. The situation has become so dire, the similarly depleted RFA is being tasked with shadowing suspected Russian shadow fleet tankers through the English Channel . Is this what getting tough on Russia looks like? Oh deary me! Our six Type 45 destroyers are elite, but getting them out at sea is increasingly a herculean effort itself (see Dragon). It’s a similar story for our two aircraft carriers which have also suffered from availability issues over the years. The number of F-35 fighter jets available to fly off the £3 billion vessels remains a bone of contention, as does the lack of British escorts. The Submarine Service also has its problems, with no operational attack boats at sea becoming an all too familiar issue. While more submarines and warships are on the horizon, the first Type 26 frigate still isn’t due to enter service until 2028. Gen Sir Gwyn this week made it clear additional vessels and drones will be needed to deter the “greatest threat” of Russia. This can only be the case with serious investment by Chancellor John Healey . Otherwise, the notion Britannia can rule the waves again will run aground. NATO chief's spending warning The head of NATO has heaped further pressure on Andy Burnham to show how Britain will meet the alliance’s spending goal. Secretary General Mark Rutte said the UK needs a “credible path” to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with increases every year. The Government has so far only budgeted to increase defence spending to 2.7% by 2027/28, with no clear details on further hikes beyond that date. The Prime Minister is increasingly being urged to hit 3% of GDP by 2030 amid fears of a possible Russian attack on NATO territory. NATO chief Mark Rutte (left) with PM Andy Burnham (Image: Getty) Chancellor John Healey said this was what needed to happen when he quit as Sir Keir Starmer ’s defence secretary. However, he has since appeared unwilling to recommit to the interim target and said he will set out the timetable for achieving 3.5% by 2035 at next year’s spending review. Mr Rutte said NATO cannot “be naive” about actions Vladimir Putin might take against the alliance. NATO 'not yet ready' for drone threat NATO allies have been warned they will struggle to fend off the kind of mass drone and missile attacks that Ukraine is doing on a daily basis. Lithuanian air force chief Colonel Antanas Matutis said the production capacities of alliance members are likely “not yet ready” to meet the threat. Drones can be produced and fired on mass as they are incredibly cheap. Air defence is a particular weakness for the British military. The Sea Viper-armed Type 45 destroyers are Britain’s only defence against ballistic missiles and, as we know, these sophisticated vessels have suffered numerous availability issues.
